body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Enhancement of phagocytosis by coating of foreign particles with serum proteins is called ...

A. agglutination.
B. chemotaxis.
C. opsonization.
D. solubilization.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. agglutination. | **F** | Clumping of particles by antibody. |
| B. chemotaxis. | **F** | Directed migration towards chemical signals. |
| C. opsonization. | **T** | Coating with opsonins (IgG, C3b) enhances phagocytosis. |
| D. solubilization. | **F** | Not the term. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Opsonins** (IgG via Fcγ receptors, C3b/iC3b via CR1/CR3, CRP, MBL) coat particles so phagocytes bind and ingest them more efficiently.

## Simplified explanation

Coating microbes with serum proteins so phagocytes eat them more easily is opsonization.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following peripheral blood cell(s) play(s) a key role in killing of parasites.

A. Eosinophils
B. Lymphocytes
C. Monocytes
D. Neutrophils
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Eosinophils | **T** | Release major basic protein and other toxic granule contents onto helminths. |
| B. Lymphocytes | **F** | They direct the response but are not the main killers. |
| C. Monocytes | **F** | Not the key anti-helminth effector. |
| D. Neutrophils | **F** | Mainly antibacterial. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Eosinophils** kill large parasites (helminths) by IgE/IgG-dependent cytotoxicity, releasing **major basic protein**, eosinophil cationic protein, peroxidase and neurotoxin; eosinophilia is typical of helminth infection.

## Simplified explanation

Eosinophils are the parasite killers.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Skin, lactic acid secretions, stomach acidity, and the motion of cilia represent ...

A. Acquired immunity
B. Adaptive immunity
C. Auto immunity
D. Natural immunity
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Acquired immunity | **F** | These barriers are present from birth. |
| B. Adaptive immunity | **F** | Not antigen-specific. |
| C. Auto immunity | **F** | Autoimmunity is reaction against self. |
| D. Natural immunity | **T** | Innate (natural) barrier defences. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Innate (natural) immunity**: physical barriers (skin, mucous membranes, cilia), chemical barriers (lactic/fatty acids, gastric acid, lysozyme), normal flora, phagocytes, NK cells, complement, inflammation. It is non-specific and has no memory.

## Simplified explanation

These are inborn, non-specific barriers: natural immunity.

body: The structure formed by the fusion of engulfed material and enzymatic granules within the phagocytic cell is called a ...

options.hint: The vesicle containing ingested material before fusion.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Phagocytosis: chemotaxis → adherence (opsonins) → ingestion forms a **phagosome** → fusion with lysosomes/granules forms the **phagolysosome** → killing (oxygen-dependent respiratory burst, oxygen-independent enzymes, defensins) → exocytosis.

## Simplified explanation

When the phagosome fuses with lysosomes it becomes a phagolysosome.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The presence of normal flora acts as a defense mechanism by ...

A. coating mucosal surfaces
B. competing with pathogens for nutrients
C. keeping phagocytes in the area
D. maintaining an acid environment
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. coating mucosal surfaces | **T** | Occupies attachment sites, preventing pathogen colonisation. |
| B. competing with pathogens for nutrients | **T** | Competitive exclusion. |
| C. keeping phagocytes in the area | **F** | Not a recognised mechanism. |
| D. maintaining an acid environment | **T** | e.g. vaginal lactobacilli produce lactic acid. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Colonisation resistance** by normal flora: competition for nutrients and attachment sites, production of acids (lactobacilli), bacteriocins and other inhibitory substances, and stimulation of the immune system. Antibiotics that disrupt flora allow overgrowth (e.g. C. difficile, Candida).

## Simplified explanation

Normal flora protect us by taking up space and nutrients and making the environment acidic.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following is/are **not** characteristic(s) of a good immunogen.

A. Found on host cells.
B. Internal complexity.
C. Large molecular weight.
D. The presence of numerous epitopes.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Found on host cells. | **T** | Self molecules are tolerated, so they are poor immunogens. |
| B. Internal complexity. | **F** | Complexity is a characteristic of a good immunogen. |
| C. Large molecular weight. | **F** | Large size (>100 kDa) favours immunogenicity. |
| D. The presence of numerous epitopes. | **F** | Many epitopes favour immunogenicity. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Properties of a good immunogen: **foreignness**, **high molecular weight** (>100,000 Da best; <10,000 poor), **chemical complexity** (proteins > polysaccharides), many epitopes, degradability (processing), and appropriate dose/route; genetics of the host also matter.

## Simplified explanation

A good immunogen is large, complex, has many epitopes and is foreign. Being found on host cells makes it a poor one.

body: Adjuvants act by which of the following methods?

options.text: Complex to antigen to increase its size
options.hint: True, but not the only mechanism.

options.text: Prevent rapid escape from the tissues
options.hint: True (depot effect), but not the only mechanism.
True, but not the only mechanism.
Correct. Adjuvants act in all these ways.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Adjuvants (alum, Freund's, MF59, TLR agonists) enhance immunogenicity by forming a **depot** for slow release, increasing antigen **size/aggregation**, promoting uptake and **processing** by APCs, and inducing local inflammation and co-stimulatory molecule expression.

## Simplified explanation

Adjuvants enlarge the antigen, keep it in the tissue longer and improve its processing.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Characteristic(s) of variable domains of immunoglobulins is/are that, they ...

A. are at the carboxy-terminal ends of the molecules.
B. have hinge regions
C. occur on both the H and L chains.
D. represent the complement binding site.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. are at the carboxy-terminal ends of the molecules. | **F** | V domains are at the **amino**-terminal ends. |
| B. have hinge regions | **F** | The hinge lies between CH1 and CH2 of heavy chains. |
| C. occur on both the H and L chains. | **T** | VH and VL form the antigen-binding site. |
| D. represent the complement binding site. | **F** | C1q binds the CH2 (IgG) or CH3 (IgM) constant domain. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Each Ig chain has an N-terminal **variable domain** (VH, VL) containing three hypervariable CDRs that form the **antigen-binding site**, and constant domains (CL; CH1–CH3/4). Effector functions (complement, Fc receptor binding) reside in the **Fc** constant region.

## Simplified explanation

Variable domains sit at the amino ends of both heavy and light chains and bind antigen; complement binds the constant region.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The subclasses of IgG differ mainly in ...

A. molecular weight.
B. the ability to act as opsonins.
C. the arrangement of disulfide bonds.
D. the type of L chain.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. molecular weight. | **F** | All are ~150 kDa (IgG3 slightly larger). |
| B. the ability to act as opsonins. | **F** | Functional differences follow from the structural difference. |
| C. the arrangement of disulfide bonds. | **T** | Number and position of inter-heavy-chain disulphide bonds (and hinge length). |
| D. the type of L chain. | **F** | All subclasses use κ or λ light chains. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

IgG1–IgG4 differ in their γ heavy chains, mainly in the **hinge region** and the number/arrangement of **inter-heavy chain disulphide bonds** (IgG1: 2, IgG2: 4, IgG3: 11, IgG4: 2). These differences affect complement activation (IgG3 > IgG1 > IgG2; IgG4 none), Fc receptor binding and half-life.

## Simplified explanation

IgG subclasses differ mostly in their disulphide bonds/hinge.

body: How many antigen binding sites does a typical IgM molecule have?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Secreted IgM is a **pentamer** of five monomers joined by J chain and disulphide bonds, giving **10 antigen-binding sites** (valency 10, effective valency often 5 for large antigens due to steric hindrance), hence high avidity and strong agglutination/complement fixation.

## Simplified explanation

IgM has five units with two binding sites each: 10.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

A Fab fragment does **not** consist of ...

A. one L chain and an entire H chain.
B. one L chain and one-half of an H chain.
C. two H chains.
D. two L chains.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. one L chain and an entire H chain. | **T** | Fab contains only part of the H chain. |
| B. one L chain and one-half of an H chain. | **F** | This is what Fab is (L chain + Fd). |
| C. two H chains. | **T** | Fab has no complete H chains. |
| D. two L chains. | **T** | Fab has one L chain. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Papain cleaves IgG above the hinge into **two Fab** fragments (each = one complete **light chain** + the **Fd** portion, VH + CH1, i.e. about half a heavy chain; one antigen-binding site) and one **Fc** fragment (two CH2–CH3 pieces). Pepsin gives one F(ab')₂.

## Simplified explanation

A Fab is one light chain plus half a heavy chain; anything else is not Fab.

body: Which of the following are L chains of antibody molecules?

options.hint: Correct. Light chains are κ or λ.
γ is the IgG heavy chain.
µ is the IgM heavy chain.
α is the IgA heavy chain.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Light chains: **κ** and **λ** (ratio ~2:1 in humans). Heavy chains define class: γ (IgG), α (IgA), µ (IgM), δ (IgD), ε (IgE).

## Simplified explanation

Light chains are kappa or lambda; Greek letters like gamma, mu and alpha name heavy chains.

body: All of the following are true of IgE except that it ...

options.hint: Correct (the exception). IgE is heat labile (inactivated at 56 °C).

options.text: is found in the serum of allergic persons.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

IgE: lowest serum concentration, binds **FcεRI** on mast cells/basophils, mediates type I hypersensitivity and anti-helminth defence, does **not** fix complement, does not cross the placenta, and is **heat labile** (loses mast-cell binding at 56 °C).

## Simplified explanation

IgE is destroyed by heat, so 'heat stable' is the false statement.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following antibody/antibodies is/are best at agglutination and complement fixation.

A. IgA
B. IgD
C. IgG
D. IgM
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. IgA | **F** | Does not activate the classical pathway. |
| B. IgD | **F** | Minimal effector function. |
| C. IgG | **F** | Good, but less efficient than IgM. |
| D. IgM | **T** | Pentameric IgM is the best agglutinator and complement fixer. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

One bound IgM pentamer can activate C1q (whereas ≥2 adjacent IgG are needed), and its 10 binding sites make it ~1000× more efficient at agglutination than IgG.

## Simplified explanation

IgM, with ten binding sites, clumps cells and activates complement best.

body: The double diffusion method allows for disease identification and diagnosis and is an application of what immunological technique?

options.hint: Correct. Soluble antigen-antibody precipitin lines in gel.

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Ouchterlony double immunodiffusion forms precipitin lines at equivalence between wells of antigen and antibody.

## Simplified explanation

Double diffusion is a precipitation method.

body: Specific immunity exhibits four characteristic attributes, which are mediated by lymphocytes. List these FOUR (4) attributes.
answer:
1. **Specificity**: each lymphocyte recognises a particular epitope.
2. **Diversity**: an enormous repertoire of receptors (~10⁹–10¹¹) recognises virtually any antigen.
3. **Memory**: a faster, stronger secondary response on re-exposure.
4. **Self/non-self discrimination** (self-tolerance).

> [!answer]
> Specificity, diversity, memory, self/non-self discrimination.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These attributes arise from clonal selection: somatic recombination of V(D)J segments generates diversity; antigen selects specific clones; some become long-lived memory cells; central and peripheral tolerance remove or silence self-reactive clones.

## Simplified explanation

Adaptive immunity is specific, diverse, has memory and can tell self from non-self.

body:
State ONE (1) immunological response the following innate immune cells are involved in:

a. Mast cells
b. Basophils
c. Eosinophils
d. Macrophages
e. Neutrophils
answer:
| Cell | Immunological response (any one) |
|---|---|
| a. Mast cells | **Inflammation/immediate (type I) hypersensitivity**: release of histamine and other mediators |
| b. Basophils | **Allergic/inflammatory reactions** (histamine release via IgE) |
| c. Eosinophils | **Killing of parasites (helminths)**; allergic inflammation |
| d. Macrophages | **Phagocytosis** and **antigen presentation**; cytokine production |
| e. Neutrophils | **Phagocytosis** of bacteria (acute inflammation) |

> [!answer]
> Mast cells and basophils: inflammation/allergy; eosinophils: anti-parasitic; macrophages: phagocytosis/antigen presentation; neutrophils: phagocytosis.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Innate effector cells recognise pathogens via pattern recognition receptors (TLRs) and Fc/complement receptors, and bridge to adaptive immunity (macrophages and dendritic cells present antigen).

## Simplified explanation

Mast cells and basophils cause inflammation and allergy, eosinophils fight parasites, and macrophages and neutrophils eat microbes.

body:
State how the following barriers help in host defense against infections:

a. Skin
b. Sebaceous glands
c. Digestive tract
d. Mucous membranes
e. Saliva
answer:
| Barrier | How it protects |
|---|---|
| a. Skin | Intact, keratinised, tightly packed epithelium forms a **physical barrier**; constant **desquamation** removes microbes; dry and slightly acidic |
| b. Sebaceous glands | Secrete **sebum** containing fatty and lactic acids that lower skin **pH (~3–5)** and inhibit bacterial growth |
| c. Digestive tract | **Gastric acid** (low pH) and digestive enzymes kill ingested microbes; peristalsis and normal flora prevent colonisation |
| d. Mucous membranes | **Mucus traps** microbes, which are swept away by **cilia**; secretions contain lysozyme and secretory IgA |
| e. Saliva | **Washes** the mouth and contains **lysozyme** (breaks bacterial cell walls), lactoferrin and IgA |

> [!answer]
> Skin: physical barrier/desquamation; sebum: acidic fatty acids; gut: acid and enzymes; mucous membranes: trap microbes (cilia, mucus); saliva: washing and lysozyme.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

First-line defences are anatomical, physiological (pH, temperature), chemical (lysozyme, defensins) and microbial (normal flora). Breaches (burns, catheters, achlorhydria, cystic fibrosis) increase infection risk.

## Simplified explanation

Each barrier blocks, traps, washes or chemically kills microbes before they can invade.

body: State any FOUR (4) relevance of inflammation.
answer:
Any four:

- **Delivers leucocytes** (neutrophils, monocytes) and plasma proteins (antibodies, complement) to the site of infection.
- **Destroys/eliminates** invading microbes.
- **Dilutes and localises** toxins and prevents spread of infection (fibrin barrier).
- **Removes** dead cells and debris.
- **Initiates tissue repair** and healing.
- Activates the **adaptive immune response** (antigen transport to lymph nodes).

> [!answer]
> Recruits immune cells, kills/contains microbes, clears debris, starts repair.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Acute inflammation: vasodilation and increased permeability (exudate), leucocyte emigration (margination, rolling, adhesion, diapedesis, chemotaxis), phagocytosis; cardinal signs rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa. Uncontrolled inflammation damages tissue.

## Simplified explanation

Inflammation brings immune cells to fight infection, contains it, cleans up the damage and starts healing.

body: Describe any THREE (3) characteristics of the Adaptive Immune System.
answer:
Any three:

- **Specificity**: lymphocyte receptors (BCR, TCR) recognise particular epitopes.
- **Diversity**: a vast receptor repertoire generated by V(D)J recombination recognises almost any antigen.
- **Memory**: memory B and T cells give a faster, stronger secondary response (basis of vaccination).
- **Self/non-self discrimination**: tolerance prevents attack on self.
- **Clonal expansion**: antigen-selected lymphocytes proliferate.
- **Specialisation/contraction**: responses are tailored (Th1, Th2, CTL, antibody classes) and wane after the antigen is cleared.

> [!answer]
> e.g. specificity, diversity and memory (with self/non-self discrimination).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Adaptive immunity is mediated by B cells (humoral) and T cells (cell-mediated); it takes days to develop on first exposure but improves with each exposure, unlike innate immunity.

## Simplified explanation

Adaptive immunity targets specific antigens, can recognise a huge variety, remembers past infections and leaves self alone.

body: Differentiate between Natural Passive Acquired Immunity and Natural Active Acquired Immunity.
answer:
- **Natural passive**: **pre-formed antibodies** are transferred naturally from another individual, e.g. **maternal IgG across the placenta** or **IgA in breast milk**; immediate but **short-lived** and no memory.
- **Natural active**: the person's own immune system produces antibodies/memory cells after **natural infection** (e.g. after measles); slower to develop but **long-lasting** with memory.

> [!answer]
> Natural passive = antibodies received from mother (placenta/milk), temporary; natural active = own response after infection, long-lasting memory.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Artificial counterparts: artificial active = vaccination; artificial passive = antitoxin/immunoglobulin injection.

## Simplified explanation

Passive: you borrow antibodies from your mother. Active: your body makes its own after an infection.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following is/are involved in adaptive immunity.

A. Sebum under the skin
B. Hair in the nose
C. HCl in the stomach
D. Bacteria on the skin
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Sebum under the skin | **F** | Innate chemical barrier. |
| B. Hair in the nose | **F** | Innate physical barrier. |
| C. HCl in the stomach | **F** | Innate chemical barrier. |
| D. Bacteria on the skin | **F** | Normal flora: innate defence. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Adaptive immunity is mediated by **lymphocytes** and their products (antibodies, cytokines). Physical/chemical barriers and normal flora are part of **innate** immunity.

## Simplified explanation

All four are innate defences, not adaptive ones.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Granulocytic immune cells include(s) ...

A. macrophages
B. neutrophils
C. basophils
D. eosinophils
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. macrophages | **F** | Mononuclear phagocytes, not granulocytes. |
| B. neutrophils | **T** | Granulocyte. |
| C. basophils | **T** | Granulocyte. |
| D. eosinophils | **T** | Granulocyte. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Granulocytes (polymorphonuclear leucocytes): **neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils** (and tissue mast cells are related). Monocytes/macrophages are mononuclear phagocytes.

## Simplified explanation

Neutrophils, basophils and eosinophils are granulocytes; macrophages are not.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In humans, MHC is found on Chromosome ...

A. 2.
B. 4.
C. 6.
D. 8.
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. 2. | **F** | κ light chain locus. |
| B. 4. | **F** | Incorrect. |
| C. 6. | **T** | HLA complex on 6p21.3. |
| D. 8. | **F** | Incorrect. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The human MHC (**HLA**) complex lies on the short arm of **chromosome 6** (6p21.3), containing class I (A, B, C), class II (DR, DQ, DP) and class III (complement C2, C4, factor B, TNF) genes.

## Simplified explanation

Human HLA genes are on chromosome 6.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

MHC genes are systematized into ...

A. MHC Class I
B. MHC Class II
C. MHC Class III
D. MHC Class IV
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. MHC Class I | **T** | HLA-A, -B, -C. |
| B. MHC Class II | **T** | HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP. |
| C. MHC Class III | **T** | Complement components, TNF, HSP70. |
| D. MHC Class IV | **F** | No class IV region. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

MHC class I (all nucleated cells; present to CD8⁺ T cells), class II (APCs; present to CD4⁺ T cells), class III (C2, C4, factor B, TNF-α/β, HSP70; not antigen-presenting).

## Simplified explanation

There are class I, II and III regions; there is no class IV.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

T-cell subsets include(s) ...

A. helper T cells
B. follicular T cells
C. cytotoxic T cells
D. suppressor T cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. helper T cells | **T** | CD4⁺ Th cells. |
| B. follicular T cells | **T** | T follicular helper (Tfh) cells help germinal-centre B cells. |
| C. cytotoxic T cells | **T** | CD8⁺ CTLs. |
| D. suppressor T cells | **T** | Regulatory (suppressor) T cells. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

T-cell subsets: CD4⁺ helper (Th1, Th2, Th17, **Tfh**), CD8⁺ **cytotoxic**, **regulatory/suppressor** (Treg), memory, γδ and NKT cells.

## Simplified explanation

All four are recognised T-cell types.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Cardinal characteristics of inflammation include(s) ...

A. Heat
B. Pain
C. Redness
D. Swelling
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Heat | **T** | Calor. |
| B. Pain | **T** | Dolor. |
| C. Redness | **T** | Rubor. |
| D. Swelling | **T** | Tumor. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Celsus' four cardinal signs: **rubor** (redness), **calor** (heat), **tumor** (swelling), **dolor** (pain); Virchow added **functio laesa** (loss of function). They result from vasodilation, increased permeability and mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin).

## Simplified explanation

Heat, pain, redness and swelling are all cardinal signs (plus loss of function).
